title: Efficient LLM-Generated Shuttling Compilers for Complex Trapped-Ion Architectures
authors: Fabian Kreppel, Reza Salkhordeh, Ferdinand Schmidt-Kaler, André Brinkmann
abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers rely on shuttling compilers, which cast an input algorithm into a sequence of ion-qubit movements within a given architecture. We present the first study in which a single frontier large language model (LLM), Claude Opus 4.7, generates and iteratively refines the full Python code of shuttling compilers from written specifications. We start with a compiler for (i) a linear segmented trap, extend it to (ii) a trap with junctions, and finally achieve efficient compilation for (iii) a broad class of connected trap graphs. The compilers for the more general cases are seeded with code from the previous ones. We benchmark the LLM-generated compilers against state-of-the-art hand-crafted ones using a common suite of quantum circuits. The number of shuttling timesteps is reduced by up to 76% for (i) and up to 39% for (ii). For the broad case (iii) of freely connected architectures, we find large variations in the required number of shuttling timesteps, depending on the connectivity. A densely connected, junction-rich architecture yields an order-of-magnitude reduction in shuttling timesteps compared to a corridor-like one. Repeating the complete generation and evaluation with a second frontier LLM, Claude Fable 5, reproduces these findings, with the Fable 5 compilers surpassing the hand-crafted ones more often on the largest circuits. Our results show that an unmodified frontier LLM can produce working, correct, and competitive shuttling compilers without additional manual algorithmic engineering, thus reducing the development time for new architectures from several months to a few days.
summary: This paper demonstrates that frontier Large Language Models can autonomously generate highly efficient shuttling compilers for complex trapped-ion quantum architectures. By treating the trap as a graph, the LLMs minimize the required ion movement time steps compared to existing methods. This capability significantly accelerates the development cycle for new quantum hardware designs.
main_problem: The core problem is developing efficient software compilers that translate abstract quantum algorithms into physical sequences of ion-qubit movements (shuttling) required by trapped-ion hardware.
main_result: Frontier LLMs can generate working, competitive shuttling compilers for complex architectures without manual algorithmic engineering, drastically reducing development time from months to days.
method: The authors used state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Opus 4.7 and Fable 5) to iteratively generate and refine Python code that maps quantum circuits onto physical trap graphs representing ion connectivity.
model_or_system: The system is a trapped-ion quantum computer, modeled as a graph where vertices are trap segments and edges represent shuttling paths. The compiler must schedule sequential movements of ions (qubits) across this graph structure.
key_observables: The primary observable is the number of shuttling timesteps required to execute a circuit; reductions up to 76% were reported compared to hand-crafted methods.
important_parameters: Architectural complexity, measured by connectivity (linear vs. junction-rich graphs), and qubit count (up to 50 qubits tested).
main_assumptions: Shuttling operations are assumed to be executed sequentially; the current focus deliberately excludes scheduling simultaneous gates across multiple segments.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the systematic, chained generation process from simple linear traps to complex general graph architectures. Figure 2 shows the structure of the resulting compiler code, highlighting LLM-written functions within a fixed framework.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the compiler by testing increasing architectural complexity: first on linear segments, then on junctions, and finally on broad classes of connected trap graphs using comprehensive test suites (T1-T14).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the crucial engineering bottleneck in trapped-ion quantum computing—the translation layer between abstract circuits and physical hardware movements—using advanced AI tools.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the approach. The three shuttling compilers are generated in a chained sequence of increasing architectural generality: from top to bottom, a linear architecture (Sec. IV), a branched architecture with junctions and stacks (Sec. V), and a general architecture (Sec. VI). Each subsequent compiler is seeded with the previous one’s optimized code together with a written specification of what must change, while the linear-architecture compiler starts from scratch. Each emitted compiler is then refined through follow-up optimization prompts that target timesteps, compile time, and memory use. Beside each stage, we draw the corresponding architecture, in which qubit segments...

Fig. 2. Structure of the single-file compiler ion_trap_compiler.py. Boxes in green are the provided, fixed components that the LLM may not change: the outer functions parse_input and validate_and_output and the data classes TrapGraph and QuantumGate. Boxes in blue are the two functions written by the LLM: initial_mapping and compile. The shaded frame groups the QuantumGate objects into the list the pipeline passes along. Solid arrows follow the compilation pipeline, and dashed lines show which data-class objects each function builds or uses. Of TrapGraph’s query methods, the figure shows only those shared by all three compilers.
